items.q: A straight line passes through the points (2, 8) and (6, 4). What is its slope?

why.correct: Slope is rise over run: $\frac{4 - 8}{6 - 2} = \frac{-4}{4} = -1$. The line falls one unit for each unit it moves right.

mistakes.why: You dropped the sign. The vertical value falls from 8 to 4 while the horizontal value rises, so the slope is negative.

items.q: As the price of a scooter rises from \$4 to \$10 (hundreds of dollars), the number sellers offer rises from 20 to 50. Price is on the vertical axis. What is the slope of the line between these points?

why.correct: Rise over run: the rise is $10 - 4 = 6$ and the run is $50 - 20 = 30$, so the slope is $\frac{6}{30} = 0.2$.

mistakes.why: You divided the run by the rise. Slope is the change in the vertical value over the change in the horizontal value: 6 / 30.

items.q: A line on a graph rises from left to right. What is true of its slope?
options: It is negative
It is positive
It is zero
It is undefined

why.correct: Rising to the right means the vertical value grows as the horizontal value grows: a positive slope.
options: A negative slope falls from left to right.
Right: both values rise together.
A zero slope is a flat line.
Rise over run gives a number for any straight line that is not vertical.

items.q: On a graph with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, a curve is a vertical line at a quantity of 50. What does it show?
options: The quantity is 50 at every price
The price is 50 at every quantity
Quantity rises as price rises
Quantity falls as price rises

why.correct: A vertical line keeps the horizontal value fixed, so the quantity stays at 50 whatever the price.
options: Right: the horizontal value never changes along a vertical line.
That would be a horizontal line at a price of 50.
That would be an upward-sloping curve.
That would be a downward-sloping curve.

items.q: What is the slope of a horizontal line?
options: One, because it runs straight across the whole graph
Negative, because it runs to the right
It changes from point to point
Zero, because the vertical value does not change

why.correct: Along a horizontal line the rise is 0 for any run, so the slope is 0.
options: A slope of 1 rises one unit for each unit across.
Running to the right does not make a slope negative; falling does.
A straight line has the same slope at every point.
Right: no rise means a slope of zero.

items.q: A straight line and a curve that bows outward both run from the vertical axis down to the horizontal axis. How do their slopes differ?
options: Both have the same slope at every point
The line gets steeper as it moves right; the bowed curve does not
The line's slope is the same at every point; the bowed curve gets steeper as it moves right
The bowed curve has a positive slope and the line a negative slope

why.correct: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve bowed outward starts flat and grows steeper as it falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: Only a straight line keeps one slope; the bowed curve changes.
This reverses them.
Right: constant for the line, steeper and steeper for the bowed curve.
Both fall from left to right, so both slopes are negative.

items.q: Using the table, what is the slope of the line, with price on the vertical axis?

why.correct: Between the first two rows the rise is $7 - 9 = -2$ and the run is $20 - 10 = 10$, so the slope is $\frac{-2}{10} = -0.2$. Any two rows give the same answer on a straight line.

mistakes.why: You dropped the sign. Price falls as quantity rises, so the slope is negative.
You divided the run by the rise. Slope is the change in price (vertical) over the change in quantity (horizontal).

items.q: How would you describe the curve drawn from the table?
options: Upward sloping: a positive slope from point to point
Downward sloping: a negative slope
A vertical line
A horizontal line

why.correct: Price falls by \$2 each time quantity rises by 10, so the line falls from left to right.
options: An upward-sloping line would show price rising with quantity.
Right: price falls as quantity rises.
A vertical line would keep the quantity fixed.
A horizontal line would keep the price fixed.

items.q: If the line from the table keeps the same slope, what price goes with a quantity of 50 sandwiches?

why.correct: Each 10 more sandwiches come with a price \$2 lower, so 50 sandwiches go with \$3 - \$2 = \$1.
options: Right: one more step of -\$2 from \$3.
That lowers the price by only \$1; each step of 10 is \$2.
That is the price at 40 sandwiches.
That lowers the price by \$3 in one step.

items.q: Place point X on the upward-sloping curve at a higher price than the marked starting point.

why.correct: Along an upward-sloping curve, a higher price goes with a larger quantity: X sits up and to the right on S.

items.q: Place point X on the downward-sloping curve at a larger quantity than the marked starting point.

why.correct: Along a downward-sloping curve, a larger quantity goes with a lower price: X sits down and to the right on D.

items.q: Using the first two rows of the table, what is the slope of line B?

why.correct: Rise $9 - 8 = 1$, run $2 - 0 = 2$, so the slope is $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$.

mistakes.why: You divided the run by the rise. Slope is the change in the vertical value over the change in the horizontal value: 1 / 2.
That is the rise alone. Divide it by the run, 2.

items.q: Which line is steeper, and how do you know?
options: Line B: it starts higher, at 8 against 2
Line B: its values are larger in the first two rows
Neither: both lines reach 10 at a horizontal value of 4
Line A: it rises 4 for every 2 across, a slope of 2

why.correct: Steepness is slope. Line A's slope is $\frac{6 - 2}{2 - 0} = 2$; line B's is $\frac{9 - 8}{2 - 0} = 0.5$.
options: Where a line starts does not set its tilt. Line B rises only 1 for every 2 across.
Larger values put a line higher on the graph. They do not make it steeper.
The lines meet at that point, but line A climbed 8 to get there and line B climbed 2.
Right: a slope of 2 is steeper than a slope of 0.5.

items.q: A student finds line A's slope from the first two rows, then again from the last two rows. What should she find?
options: A larger slope from the last two rows
A smaller slope from the last two rows
The same slope, 2, from both pairs of rows
A negative slope from the last two rows

why.correct: A straight line has the same slope at every point: $\frac{6 - 2}{2 - 0} = 2$ and $\frac{10 - 6}{4 - 2} = 2$.
options: A slope that grows along the way belongs to a curve, not to a straight line.
A slope that shrinks along the way belongs to a curve, not to a straight line.
Right: any two points on a straight line give the same rise over run.
Line A rises to the right in every row, so its slope stays positive.

items.q: A line falls to the right through (1, 9) and (4, 3). A student writes its slope as $\frac{3 - 9}{1 - 4} = 2$. What went wrong?
options: The top and bottom were subtracted in different orders
The rise and the run were swapped in the fraction
Nothing: a line through these points has a slope of 2
The slope of a falling line is always zero

why.correct: Subtract second point minus first point both times: $\frac{3 - 9}{4 - 1} = \frac{-6}{3} = -2$. A line that falls to the right has a negative slope.
options: Right: the top is second minus first, but the bottom is first minus second, which flips the sign.
The rise is on top and the run is on the bottom. The slip is the order of subtraction in the run.
The line falls to the right, so a positive slope cannot be right.
Zero is the slope of a horizontal line. This line falls 2 for each unit to the right.

items.q: Why does a vertical line have no rise-over-run number for its slope?
options: Its rise is zero, so the slope is zero
Its run is zero, and you cannot divide by zero
Its slope is negative at every point
Its slope changes from point to point

why.correct: Between any two points on a vertical line the horizontal value does not change, so the run is zero and rise over run cannot be computed.
options: A rise of zero describes a horizontal line, whose slope is zero.
Right: the horizontal value stays the same, so the run is zero.
A negative slope belongs to a line that falls to the right.
A changing slope belongs to a curve. A vertical line is straight.
